newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Belgian air show death toll rises to nine.
newsitem.headline: Belgian air show death toll rises to nine.

text.p: The death toll from a plane crash at an airshow in the Belgian coastal town of Ostend rose to nine after a 19-year-old Belgian Red Cross worker died in hospital on Sunday afternoon, Belga news agency reported.
The other eight victims were killed immediately when the light plane mounting an aerobatics display crashed onto a Red Cross tent on Saturday at around five p.m. (1500 GMT).
The pilot, 28-year-old Captain Amr Hani Bilal of Jordan's Royal Falcons aerobatics display team, was among those who died in the crash.

A Frenchman and his 22-month-old daughter and five Belgian men, most in their late twenties and early thirties also died, Joan Dewinne, head of the special disaster victim identification unit, told a news conference in Ostend earlier on Sunday.
Dewinne said they all died on impact. "Their death was immediate, that is clear." Burning fuel from the plane then heavily charred their bodies, hampering identification.
The Jordanian air force aerobatics plane spun out of control during a solo display and crashed, raining debris on the crowd and spraying people with burning fuel.
Thirty of the 57 injured have been able to return home, Belgian Interior Minister Johan Vande Lanotte told Reuters in Ostend. The health of two of the critically ill stabilised on Sunday.
"The plane flew directly over the crowd, which is not allowed," he said.
Air show rules dictate that a display must be interrupted when a plane crosses the so-called display line, usually the runway, and flies immediately over the spectators.
Belgian radio said the circumstances pointed to pilot error.

Guy Debarbieux, for the organisers of the airshow, said all safety regulations had been followed. "We have the instructions of the aviation administration and we follow them strictly," he told reporters.
A Belgian aviation expert said the German-made Falcon XT 300 had failed to pull up, which could point to mechanical failure.

Alternatively, the pilot could have passed out during a series of horizontal spins which involve great strain on plane and pilot from the forces of gravity. "There appears to have been no reaction by the pilot," he said.
Eyewitness Patrick Beugnies told Reuters: "I saw one small plane make strange movements about 100 metres away. It crashed, there was a sea of flames and thick black smoke."
It fell on a first aid post at the edge of the spectator area. "My father, standing next to me, saw the white canvas fly up and then there were flames...nothing was left of the plane."
Asked on Belgian radio whether safety rules had been obeyed, Vande Lanotte said: "For as far we can see now, yes."
Ostend airport director Luc Van Bouwel told Reuters he had been worried about holding air shows at civil airports. "I think this kind of show is better performed at a military base."

Sunday's displays at the two-day show in Ostend were cancelled because of the crash but a show in the eastern Belgian town of Hechtel went ahead as planned, attracting 20,000 spectators. Organisors said safety measures were stepped up.
King Albert and Queen Paola interrupted their holidays in Italy and flew back to Belgium to join Prime Minister Jean-Luc Dehaene to pay their respects to the dead at an Ostend mortuary.
They were joined by members of the Royal Falcons team and the Jordanian ambassador in Belgium, Amaya Toucan.
"We are 11, now we are 10," a team member said. The Falcons would not fly at Hechtel, but return to Jordan later on Sunday.
Toucan said the dead pilot, married without children, would be flown home on a special flight later on Sunday.
In the world's worst air show disaster at Ramstein, Germany, in August 1988, 70 people died when three Italian jets collided in mid-air. One burst into flames and ploughed into the crowd.
